Every limerick has five lines..why: The defining feature of the form, stated in every definition.

sources.quote: It is written in five-line, predominantly anapestic and amphibrach trimeter with a strict rhyme scheme of AABBA, in which the first, second and fifth lines rhyme, while the third and fourth ones are shorter and share a different rhyme.

'The Ferryman of Fowey' has five lines..why: The title is made up for the prompt, so no text says how many lines it has; people do say that limericks have five lines, and the count for this poem is read off that rule alone.

A limerick with three lines written need.why: People say a limerick has five lines, but nobody works out how many are left after three; the number of missing lines is arithmetic on the rule, never written down.

sources.note: Read hits describe the rhyme of particular lines, not lines still to write.

Four limericks have 20 lines of verse in.why: People say a limerick has five lines; nobody states the total for four limericks, which occurs only as a count of poems, so 20 is computed from the rule.

sources.note: Read hits count poems, never their lines.

Edward Lear wrote limericks..why: Lear is the poet best known for limericks; Wikipedia says he popularised the form, and his Book of Nonsense is a volume of limericks.

sources.quote: Edward Lear (12 May 1812 – 29 January 1888) was an English artist, illustrator, musician, author and poet, who is known mostly for his literary nonsense in poetry and prose and especially his limericks, a form he popularised but which term he never used.
In 1846, Lear published The Book of Nonsense, a volume of limericks which went through three editions and helped popularise the form and the genre of literary nonsense.

sources.note: Approximate co-occurrence (AND within a window, max_clause_freq 500000), not statements of the fact.

Every limerick is written in Latin..why: Deliberately false side fact for the disjunction: the limerick is an English form, which Wikipedia places in England in the early 18th century.

sources.quote: A limerick ... is a form of verse that appeared in England in the early years of the 18th century.
sources.note: Quote taken from the review's check of the article lead (Wikipedia API rate-limited on 2026-11-12, not re-fetched).

notes: Dev TBox contraction, paired with the revision literature_arts-replace-d005 (README, Contraction: 'The three operations are paired'): it removes the same rule, 'Every limerick has five lines', which every model holds and which has no exception in the standard form. It replaces the earlier contraction of a Shakespearean-sonnet rule (the pairing rule was added to the README on 2026-11-11). The derived queries are the revision's own (a made-up 2025 limerick named in the prompt, a limerick being written, a page of four new limericks), so the two records can be compared item by item: inheritance, 2 hops, with the line count and two applications that compute with it (fol, arithmetic); after the removal each is 'does not know'. Under strong Kleene logic the three propositional answers are unknown. Determinacy problem, recorded for the user (the same kind the review raised on the earlier sonnet rule): the limerick's stored rhyme scheme AABBA (has_rhyme_scheme, a separate rule) names five lines, and 'a five-line poem' is part of most definitions, so a model can keep 'five' through another stored rule without the removal having failed. The pairing fixes which rule is removed, so no line-count question avoids this; read the derived scores with that in mind. Unrelated near asks the line count of another short fixed form (the haiku), which the removal leaves alone; contraction is exempt from Rule 7. Tag for analysis (review 2026-11-12): this is a DEFINITIONAL removal. 'Five lines' is part of what 'limerick' means and is restated by the separately stored rhyme scheme AABBA, so the 'does not know' target asks a model to keep the word while losing a defining property, and a surviving 'five' on the direct, paraphrase and derived queries is not a plain failure of the method. Slice contraction results on this record as definitional, as the geography oxbow-lake template does. The determinacy label stays 'determinate' (the dev split has no indeterminate queries and no worlds); the label is a convention for the scorer, not a claim that no other route to 'five' exists. The pairing with replace-d005 fixes the rule, so a TBox pair on a rule outside the class's definition would be needed to avoid this.
